title: The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake
subtitle: Thirty-Four Years Trekking Across China · Pilgrimage to Over Eighty National Heritage Sites
description: Xu Hongzu (Xu Xiake), Ming-dynasty geographer, traveler, and writer. Starting at age twenty-two, he spent thirty-four years trekking on foot through what are now 21 provinces and regions, leaving behind over 600,000 words in his Travel Diaries. Known as the "Eternal Wanderer." This route follows the Sage of Travel's footsteps, linking over eighty nationally protected heritage sites he visited.

route.title: The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake: Thirty-Four Years Trekking Across China's National Heritage
route.intro:
A true man should ride the morning tide on the azure sea and rest by evening beneath the verdant wutong trees.
Xu Hongzu (1587–1641), styled Xiake, was born in Jiangyin, South Zhili (present-day Jiangyin, Jiangsu). In the thirty-fifth year of the Wanli reign (1607), at the age of twenty-two, Xu Xiake set out from his hometown and began a thirty-four-year trek. He made four long-distance journeys, his footsteps covering what are now Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Jiangxi, Fujian, Henan, Shandong, Shaanxi, Hubei, Hunan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Yunnan, Shanxi, Hebei, and Beijing—21 provinces and regions in total. He is the greatest traveler in Chinese history. The first day of Xu Xiake's Travel Diaries (May 19, 1613) has been designated China Tourism Day. With a scientific spirit, he investigated landforms, hydrology, and vegetation; his records of karst landscapes, Danxia landforms, and volcanic geothermal features were centuries ahead of the rest of the world. Let us follow the Sage of Travel's footsteps, from the watery landscapes of Jiangnan to the southwestern borderlands, from the Five Sacred Mountains to the landscapes of Guilin, embarking on a journey across three centuries to visit the nationally protected heritage sites that witnessed his legendary travels.

stops.title: Stop One: Jiangyin—The Sage of Travel's Hometown
stops.content: Xu Xiake, born Hongzu, styled Xiake, was born in the fifteenth year of the Wanli reign (1587) into a scholarly family in Jiangyin. As a child, he had little interest in the Four Books and Five Classics, but he devoured the Classic of Mountains and Seas and the Commentary on the Water Classic. After his father passed away, he said to his mother: "A true man should ride the morning tide on the azure sea and rest by evening beneath the verdant wutong trees"—he had to go out and see with his own eyes the mountains and rivers described in books. In the spring of his twenty-second year, he shouldered his pack and set out—a journey that would last thirty-four years. The old house where he was born still stands—a three-courtyard Ming-dynasty compound, now the Xu Xiake Former Residence and Qingshan Hall Stone Inscriptions. The Qingshan Hall on the property was where he once studied; the stone inscriptions before the hall record the interactions between the Xu family and literary luminaries. Standing on the banks of the Yangtze in Jiangyin, watching the river roll eastward—that young man who left home with a small bundle probably never imagined that this journey would make him the Eternal Wanderer.

buildings.n: Xu Xiake's Former Residence and Qingshan Hall Stone Carvings

stops.title: Stop Two: Nanjing—The Southern Cultural Hub of Letters
stops.content: In the thirty-fifth year of the Wanli reign (1607), twenty-two-year-old Xu Xiake traveled eastward along the Yangtze; his first stop was Nanjing—the Ming auxiliary capital, the ancient capital of six dynasties. He first paid homage at the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum, the tomb of Ming founder Zhu Yuanzhang. Its scale was breathtaking; the stone statues lining the Sacred Way had stood silent guard for over a century. Then he climbed the Nanjing City Wall; from atop the gate tower, the Qinhuai River wound like a silk ribbon, and distant Zhongshan Mountain rose majestically. During his days in Nanjing, he also went outside the city to see the thousand-and-five-hundred-year-old Nanjing Southern Dynasties Imperial Tomb Stone Carvings, and visited the Qixia Temple Relic Pagoda on Qixia Mountain, a Southern Tang stone pagoda of exquisite craftsmanship. This trip to Nanjing made the young Xu Xiake truly feel—the world outside the study was even more splendid than what the books described.

buildings.n: Stone Carvings from Nanjing Southern Dynasty Tombs

stops.title: Stop Three: Zhenjiang and Yangzhou—Two Sides of the Yangtze
stops.content: Leaving Nanjing and traveling north along the Grand Canal, he reached Zhenjiang and Yangzhou. The two cities were a study in contrasts—Zhenjiang guarding the Yangtze's strategic pass, Yangzhou leaning on the canal's bustling docks. At Zhenjiang, he climbed Jiaoshan and spent half a day exploring the Jiaoshan Stele Forest, its steles spanning from the Six Dynasties to the Republic of China. Crossing the river to Yangzhou, he wandered through the Ge Garden and the He Garden. Yangzhou was different from Zhenjiang—the waters softer, the dialect sweeter, merchants and scholars from north and south brushing shoulders in lively throngs.

stops.title: Stop Four: Suzhou—The City of Gardens
stops.content: In the Ming dynasty, Suzhou was already the most prosperous city in Jiangnan. Xu Xiake visited all of Suzhou's famous gardens—the Humble Administrator's Garden, with its exquisite water features where pavilions and terraces are all built beside the water, the view changing with every step. The neighboring Lingering Garden offered a completely different flavor, with its labyrinthine rockeries built from Taihu stones. There was also the Yuan-dynasty Lion Grove Garden and the delicate Master of the Nets Garden. Suzhou had more than gardens. He climbed the gently leaning Yunyan Temple Pagoda, a Northern Song brick pagoda overlooking two and a half millennia of Suzhou's history. On the canal, the Baodai Bridge stretched fifty-three arches over three hundred meters, grain boats passing under it—a vibrant picture of life in Jiangnan.

stops.title: Wuxi and Yixing—Pearls of Lake Tai
stops.content: Wuxi borders Jiangyin, and Xu Xiake visited several times. The Garden for Ease of Mind at the foot of Huishan was built by Qin Jin, the Minister of War. It cleverly borrowed the scenery of the entire Huishan and Xishan ranges into its own garden. Nearby, the Donglin Academy was where the Donglin faction lectured; Gu Xiancheng's famous line "the sound of wind and rain, the sound of reading" once echoed through the land. On Huishan, the Second Spring Under Heaven Courtyard and Stone Inscriptions was the spring rated second best under heaven by the Tea Sage Lu Yu; Su Shi came here to drink tea and write poetry. Xu Xiake sat by the spring and had tea too, chatting with the mountain monks—perfect contentment.

buildings.n: Tianxia Second Spring Courtyard and Stone Carvings

stops.title: Stop Five: Lake Tai—Three Myriad Six Hundred Hectares of Misty Waves
stops.content: Setting out from Wuxi, he sailed on Lake Tai—three myriad six hundred hectares of misty waves, seventy-two peaks appearing and disappearing in the haze. In his travel diary, he meticulously recorded Lake Tai's hydrology and the scenery along its shores. Facing the vast expanse of misty water, the twenty-four-year-old Xu Xiake felt for the first time the magnificent grandeur of "so lovely are the rivers and mountains."

stops.title: Stop Six: Hangzhou—The Finest Scenery in the Southeast
stops.content: West Lake in Hangzhou was world-famous. He climbed the Liuhe Pagoda by the Qiantang River and looked into the distance—the river like a silver ribbon winding its way to the sea. Before Lingyin Temple, he was deeply captivated by the Feilaifeng Sculptures (including Southern Hill Sculptures)—the Yuan-dynasty stone carvings were remarkably lifelike. He made a special trip to pay homage at the Yue Fei Tomb; incense never ceased at King Yue's Temple, and the kneeling statues of Qin Hui were forever fixed on the pillar of shame—loyalty and treachery, good and evil, history has its own judgment.

stops.title: Stop Seven: Shaoxing—The Scholarly Vein of a Water Town
stops.content: Shaoxing is an ancient city that floats on water. He paid homage at the Mausoleum of Yu the Great, the tomb of the flood-control hero of four thousand years ago, nestled at the foot of Kuaiji Mountain. He searched for the Orchid Pavilion—where Wang Xizhi wrote the "Best Calligraphy Under Heaven" during the Eastern Jin, the elegant custom of floating wine cups along a winding stream capturing his imagination. He passed over the Shaoxing Ancient Bridge Cluster (including the Eight-Character Bridge), where black-canopied boats glide beneath Southern Song stone bridges—this kind of living heritage is more moving than any grand architecture.

stops.title: Stop Eight: Tiantai Mountain—Where the Travel Diaries Begin
stops.content: On the thirtieth day of the third month of the forty-first year of the Wanli reign (May 19, 1613), Xu Xiake set out for Tiantai Mountain. This day is now China Tourism Day—because this was the first entry in the Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake. He entered the Guoqing Temple, the ancestral temple of the Tiantai school of Buddhism founded in the Sui dynasty. The Sui-dynasty pagoda and Sui-dynasty plum tree within the temple have witnessed 1,400 years of history. He twice climbed Huading Peak in search of the source of the Stone Beam Waterfall—a natural stone beam spanning two cliffs, the waterfall thundering beneath. His relentless pursuit of the source is the reason Xu Xiake's Travel Diaries are still respected in the field of geography today.

stops.title: Stop Nine: Yandang Mountain—The Finest Mountain in the Southeast
stops.content: After visiting Tiantai Mountain, Xu Xiake rushed to Yandang Mountain. Here, the volcanic rhyolite landform created unique peaks and strange rocks. He risked climbing sheer cliffs to find the source of the Great Dragon Waterfall—nearly two hundred meters high, one of China's four most famous waterfalls. Spirit Peak transforms mysteriously under moonlight, like a dreamscape. His investigation of the volcanic rhyolite landform predated European scientists by more than three hundred years.

stops.title: Stop Ten: Mount Huangshan—No Need to See Other Mountains After the Five Sacred Peaks
stops.content: In the second month of the forty-fourth year of the Wanli reign (1616), Xu Xiake climbed Mount Huangshan in snow. He wrote the immortal line "After seeing the Five Sacred Peaks, no other mountain is worth seeing; after seeing Huangshan, even the Five Sacred Peaks are not worth seeing." This made Huangshan the most remarkable mountain in the Chinese imagination. The Mount Huangshan Climbing Ancient Paths and Ancient Buildings wind from Ciguang Pavilion to Beihai, blending seamlessly with the wondrous pines and strange rocks. He risked the ascent to Celestial Capital Peak—"using both hands and feet, climbing up through stone crevices"—but the view from the summit made all the effort worthwhile. In the first year of the Chongzhen reign (1628), he visited Huangshan again, and is likely the first person in the world to have recorded the granite landforms of Huangshan.

buildings.n: Huangshan Mountain Ancient Climbing Path and Ancient Buildings

stops.title: Stop Eleven: Mount Lu—The Most Beautiful Mountain Under Heaven
stops.content: In the forty-sixth year of the Wanli reign (1618), Xu Xiake came to Mount Lu. He visited the White Deer Grotto Academy, one of the Four Great Academies, made famous by Zhu Xi's lectures there. He hiked to the Three-Fold Spring, where the waterfall drops in three tiers for a total of 155 meters, spraying water like broken jade and flying snow. His investigation of Mount Lu's geology and landforms was remarkably precise.

stops.title: Stop Twelve: Mount Wuyi—Azure Water and Vermilion Mountains
stops.content: In the forty-seventh year of the Wanli reign (1619), Xu Xiake arrived at Mount Wuyi in Fujian. The red-brown Danxia landform mountains were spectacular against the surrounding azure waters. He took a bamboo raft down the Nine-Bend Stream and examined the Chencun Han City Site—a Western Han Minyue kingdom covering 480,000 square meters. Most mysterious were the Mount Wuyi Cliff Tomb Cluster, "boat coffins lodged in cliff crevices"—the ancient Yue people's hanging coffin burial custom. How they placed the coffins on cliffs tens of meters high remains a mystery to this day.

stops.title: Stop Thirteen: Mount Song—The Center of Heaven and Earth
stops.content: In the third year of the Tianqi reign (1623), Xu Xiake traveled north to Mount Song, the Central Sacred Peak. He climbed the Songyue Temple Pagoda—China's oldest surviving brick pagoda and the only twelve-sided pagoda in the country, standing firm for 1,500 years through wind and rain. At the Shaolin Temple—the ancestral temple of Chan Buddhism and the birthplace of Shaolin martial arts. He also examined the Han-dynasty Taishi Que, Shaoshi Que, and Qimu Que—some of the oldest surviving stone gate-towers in China. He also visited the Songyang Academy and the Astronomical Observatory built by Guo Shoujing.

stops.title: Kaifeng—Dreams of the Eastern Capital
stops.content: From the Central Peak he traveled west to Luoyang. He visited the Longmen Grottoes—over 2,000 niches and more than 100,000 Buddha images, with the seventeen-meter Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple, said to have been modeled after Empress Wu Zetian. He also went to the White Horse Temple—the first Buddhist monastery built after Buddhism was introduced to China; the story of "a white horse carrying sutras" has been told for nearly two thousand years.

stops.title: Stop Fourteen: Luoyang and Kaifeng—Ancient Capitals of the Central Plain
stops.content: From Luoyang he traveled east to Kaifeng. He climbed the Youguo Temple Pagoda—the Northern Song glazed-brick pagoda called the Iron Pagoda for its brown iron-like hue. He also ascended the Kaifeng City Wall and looked down over the ancient city, visited the Xiangguo Temple, and admired the exquisite brick, wood, and stone carvings at the Shan-Shaan-Gan Guild Hall.

buildings.n: Qufu Confucius Temple and Confucius Mansion

stops.title: Stop Fifteen: Mount Tai—The Supreme of the Five Sacred Peaks
stops.content: In the third year of the Tianqi reign (1623), Xu Xiake traveled east to Mount Tai—the head of the Five Sacred Peaks. Starting from the Dai Temple, the mural "The God of Mount Tai's Departure and Return Procession" in the Tiankuang Hall was magnificent in scale. Following the climbing path up, the Mount Tai Ancient Architecture Complex stretched over ten kilometers from the foot to the summit. He paused at the Southern Heavenly Gate and gazed into the distance from the Jade Emperor Summit—the grand vista stirred his blood. He also sought out the Lingyan Temple in Jinan—one of the four great temples under heaven—then traveled south to Qufu to pay homage at the Qufu Confucius Temple and Confucius Mansion and the Confucius Forest, feeling the millennium-long transmission of Confucian culture in the sage's hometown.

stops.title: Stop Sixteen: Mount Hua—The Most Perilous Peak Under Heaven
stops.content: In the first year of the Chongzhen reign (1628), Xu Xiake traveled west to Mount Hua. He ventured along the Plank Walk in the Sky—a path less than half a meter wide above a ten-thousand-zhang chasm. Below Mount Hua lay Chang'an. He studied the Xi'an Stele Forest—over four thousand steles forming a treasure house of calligraphy; climbed the Xi'an City Wall to look down over the ancient capital of thirteen dynasties; and paid homage at the Great Wild Goose Pagoda—built by Xuanzang to house the Buddhist scriptures he brought from India.

stops.title: Stop Seventeen: Wudang Mountains—A Sacred Daoist Realm
stops.content: After visiting Songshan and Huashan, he traveled south to Hubei and climbed the Wudang Mountains. The Wudang Mountains Architecture Complex stretches unbroken from the mountain foot to the Golden Summit—the Golden Hall is China's largest gilded bronze hall, the Purple Cloud Palace is magnificent, and the South Cliff Palace hangs from a sheer precipice. Ming Emperor Chengzu spent twelve years building the Wudang complex. When Xu Xiake reached the Golden Summit, he was full of praise for the splendor of the Purple Cloud Palace.

stops.title: Stop Eighteen: Mount Heng—Uniquely Beautiful in the South
stops.content: In the ninth year of the Chongzhen reign (1636), the fifty-one-year-old Xu Xiake began his astonishing "ten-thousand-mile expedition"—through Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Hunan, Guangxi, Guizhou, and Yunnan, covering the southwestern half of China. He traveled south along the Xiang River to Mount Heng. The Southern Sacred Peak Temple is one of the largest ancient architectural complexes in southern China. He summited Zhurong Peak and also went to the Yuelu Academy in Changsha to feel the millennial pulse of scholarship. On the shores of Lake Dongting, he climbed the Yueyang Tower, where Fan Zhongyan's lines "worry before the world's worries" have echoed for a thousand years.

stops.title: Stop Nineteen: Guilin—The Finest Scenery Under Heaven
stops.content: In the tenth year of the Chongzhen reign (1637), Xu Xiake entered Guilin, Guangxi. Karst peaks rose in forest-like formations, surrounded by azure waters. He toured the Jingjiang Prince's Mansion and Tombs—a Ming princely palace built thirty-four years earlier than the Forbidden City. He examined the Lingqu Canal—dug by Qin Shihuang to connect the Xiang and Li Rivers. The Guilin Stone Inscriptions are scattered across Longyin Rock and Diecai Mountain, with hundreds of Tang and Song cliff carvings. The Zengpiyan Site is a Neolithic cave dwelling. The eighty-three kilometers of the Li River form the most beautiful landscape poetry he ever wrote.

stops.title: Stop Twenty: Guizhou—The Secret Realm of Karst
stops.content: In the eleventh year of the Chongzhen reign (1638), Xu Xiake entered Guizhou. The karst landscape was spectacular—caves, underground rivers, and sinkholes were everywhere, his records predating European studies by more than two hundred years. In Guiyang, he climbed the Wenchang Pavilion and Jiaxiu Tower and searched for the Yangming Cave and Yangming Shrine—where Wang Yangming achieved enlightenment at Longchang. In Anshun, he saw China's largest waterfall, Huangguoshu, and visited the Anshun Confucian Temple and the Tiantai Mountain Wulong Temple, perched atop the mountain peak.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-One: Kunming—A Sea of Flowers in the Spring City
stops.content: Entering Yunnan, he reached Kunming. He climbed Mingfeng Mountain to see the Taihe Palace Golden Hall—China's largest extant pure bronze palace. He visited the Zhenqing Temple Ancient Architecture Complex, a Ming-dynasty Daoist building group, and soaked in the hot springs at the Hot Spring Cliff Inscriptions at Anning. By Dianchi Lake, gazing at the Western Hills in the distance—the vastness of Dianchi was breathtakingly beautiful.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Two: Dali—Wind, Flowers, Snow, and Moon
stops.content: From Kunming he traveled west to Dali. The ancient city between Cangshan Mountain and Erhai Lake was once the capital of the Nanzhao and Dali Kingdoms. The Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple stand in a tripod formation, the main pagoda, "Thousand-Seek Pagoda," reaching sixty-nine meters. The Taihe City Site (including the Nanzhao Dehua Stele) was the Nanzhao royal capital. The Xizhou Bai Ethnic Architecture Complex features whitewashed walls, black tiles, and carved beams. Drifting on Erhai Lake, gazing up at Cangshan Mountain—this scene belongs in heaven.

buildings.n: Xizhou Bai Ethnic Ancient Architecture Complex

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Three: Lijiang—Ancient Naxi Charm
stops.content: In the twelfth year of the Chongzhen reign (1639), Xu Xiake came to Lijiang. The Naxi chieftain Mu Zeng welcomed him warmly; the two hit it off immediately, drinking and talking of the world. Lijiang's ancient town was "a dense cluster of dwellings winding along the slopes and valleys." He stayed as a guest at the Mu Mansion and visited the Black Dragon Pool Ancient Architecture Complex north of the city; the Moon-Gaining Pavilion reflected in the water was like a painting. With Mu Zeng's help, he compiled the Gazetteer of Jizu Mountain. He was the first scholar from the interior to pay attention to Naxi culture.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Four: Jizu Mountain—A Buddhist Holy Land
stops.content: From Lijiang he traveled south to Jizu Mountain in Binchuan—the bodhimanda of the Buddha's disciple Mahakasyapa, where Han Buddhism and Tibetan Buddhism converge. He stayed for several months compiling the Gazetteer of Jizu Mountain, carefully surveying the mountain's water systems and drawing topographic maps. In the thirteenth year of the Chongzhen reign (1640), Xu Xiake's feet were both crippled by illness. Mu Zeng sent eight strong men to carry him on a litter for over 150 days back to his hometown of Jiangyin. The following year, the great traveler died at home, entrusting his manuscripts to a close friend—these would become the Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake, passed down through the ages.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Five: Tengchong—The Furthest Frontier City
stops.content: In the twelfth year of the Chongzhen reign (1639), Xu Xiake reached the furthest point of his life—Tengchong. He spent over forty days investigating the volcanic and geothermal phenomena. The traces of the eruption of Daying Mountain three hundred years earlier were stark and shocking; the temperature of the Boiling Pot in the Hot Sea reached over ninety degrees Celsius. He was one of the earliest travelers in the world to record volcanic geothermal features, and his description of the Tengchong volcanic cluster is considered China's first scientific survey report on volcanoes.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Six: Mount Wutai and Mount Heng—Northern Buddhist Charm (Supplementary)
stops.content: In the sixth year of the Chongzhen reign (1633), Xu Xiake traveled north to Shanxi. Mount Wutai is the bodhimanda of Manjusri Bodhisattva; the temple cluster at Taihuai Town was resplendent with gold and green. He went to Datong to see the Yungang Grottoes—forty-five caves with over 50,000 Buddha images, the pinnacle of Buddhist rock art. He visited the Huayan Temple and Shanhua Temple, and climbed the Hanging Temple on Mount Heng, suspended as if in midair. He passed by the Yingxian Wooden Pagoda—the world's tallest wooden pagoda. Traveling south to Pingyao, he examined the Pingyao City Wall—the best-preserved Ming-Qing county town wall.

stops.title: Stop Twenty-Seven: The Imperial Capital—Northern Hub (Supplementary)
stops.content: In the second year of the Chongzhen reign (1629), Xu Xiake traveled north to the imperial capital. He paid homage at the Temple of Heaven—where Ming and Qing emperors worshipped Heaven; the Forbidden City—whose grandeur stunned him. He went to the Thirteen Ming Tombs in Changping—where thirteen Ming emperors lie in eternal rest. He toured the Zhihua Temple—a Ming-dynasty wooden monastery famous for its coffered ceiling; climbed the Ancient Observatory—which fascinated this geography lover. He admired the Southeast Corner Tower of Beijing City Wall and the Zhengyang Gate to experience the majesty of the capital's defenses. Passing through Juyong Pass, he climbed the Badaling Great Wall—the dragon winding along the mountain crest stirred his heart. At this point, the Sage of Travel's footsteps had already covered most of China, and his thirty-four-year trek stands as one of the greatest feats in the history of human exploration.

buildings.n: Southeast Corner Tower of Beijing City
